newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany weighs converting old debt to Euros early.
newsitem.headline: Germany weighs converting old debt to Euros early.

text.p: Germany is weighing the idea of converting its existing government bonds to Euros at the very start of the planned single European currency, a top finance ministry official said.
"Nothing has been decided, but we are moving in this direction," finance state secretary Juergen Stark said in an interview published in the Boersen-Zeitung on Tuesday.

Bundesbank deputy president Johann Gaddum warned separately that Germany should convert its old debt to euros at the launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999. A failure to do so could lead to a split in European capital markets, to the detriment of Germany, he said.

The European Commission decided last December in Madrid that new government borrowings for EMU members should be denominated in euros when the single currency is introduced, but no decision was made in Madrid about converting existing debt to euros.
France is the only country which so far has said it will convert all its old debt to euros at the launch date.

Stark said a side agreement had originally been made for old debt to be redenominated either during or at the end of a proposed three-year transition period to convert all notes and coins to the euro.
Gaddum said the disappearance of exchange rates as an adjustment mechanism may accentuate the differences in investors' and rating agencies' perceptions of the relative quality of different issuers.
Interest rates will still vary from country to country depending on the quality of the issuer, but the currency will be the same.
Stark said Germany was aware of the consequences for Germany as a financial market and for Bonn as the benchmark issuer in the European capital market.
